theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between brazing and fusion welding?
options: In brazing the parts are always held with rivets or screws as well
In brazing both parent metals melt and flow into one pool
In brazing only the filler melts; the parent metal stays solid
In brazing the filler goes on cold and sets like a glue

questions.stem: Brazing filler metals melt above about which temperature? (Below it, the process is called soft soldering.)
What draws the melted filler metal into a close-fitting brazed joint?
options: The pressure of the gas coming out of the nozzle
The weight of the filler pulling it downwards
The magnetism of the hot steel parent metal
Capillary action between the two close surfaces

questions.stem: 'Silver soldering' is the everyday name for which process?
options: Soft soldering with a tin and lead solder
Brazing with a filler that contains silver
Fusion welding of silver with a gas flame
Plating a thin silver coat onto a part

questions.stem: Before starting a brazing job, what should you read first to find the metals, the joint type and the sizes?
options: The job drawing and the work instructions
The safety sign on the workshop door
The filler rod packet from a past job
The test date stamped on the gas cylinder

questions.stem: Which eye protection is suitable for most oxy-fuel brazing and silver soldering?
options: Clear safety glasses with no tint or filter at all
An arc welding helmet with a shade 13 filter
Tinted goggles or a visor of about shade 3 to 5
Ordinary dark sunglasses from a shop

questions.stem: Why must brazing be done in a well-ventilated area?
options: So that the flame burns with a longer, softer cone
To carry flux and metal fumes away from your face
So that the joint cools faster and does not crack
To keep the gas hoses cool so that they do not soften

questions.stem: Some older silver brazing alloys contain cadmium. Why is this a concern?
options: Cadmium makes the joint too weak for copper pipe
Cadmium stops the flux from working on steel
Cadmium makes the alloy melt at a much higher heat
Cadmium fumes are very toxic and harm the lungs

questions.stem: Heating brass or brass filler can give off zinc fumes. What illness can breathing them cause?
options: Metal fume fever, with flu-like shivers and aches
Arc eye, with sore, gritty and watering eyes at night
Sunburn on the face and neck from the flame
Hearing loss from the roar of the torch

questions.stem: What should be done before brazing near anything that can burn?
options: Spray the area with oil to keep the dust down
Cover it with a cotton cloth and carry on
Move it away or shield it, with an extinguisher close
Work faster with a bigger flame so heat cannot spread

questions.stem: Why must oil and grease never be used on oxygen regulators, fittings or hoses?
options: Oil makes the gauge needles stick and read too high
Oil and grease can catch fire or explode in oxygen
Oil blocks the filter in the flashback arrestor
Oil makes the hose slip off the fitting

questions.stem: How should an acetylene cylinder be kept while it is in use?
options: Lying on its side so the gas flows out evenly
Upside down, so that the acetone stays near the valve
Leaning against a warm wall out of the rain
Upright, and chained or strapped so it cannot fall

questions.stem: What is the job of a flashback arrestor on an oxy-fuel set?
options: To light the gas when the torch valve is opened
To raise the gas pressure for bigger nozzles
To stop a flame burning back to the cylinder
To show how much gas is still left in the cylinder

questions.stem: How should you check the gas connections for leaks after setting up?
options: Brush on soapy water and look for bubbles
Hold a lit spark lighter near each joint in turn
Smell each joint closely while the gas flows
Listen for a hiss with the cylinder valves shut

questions.stem: Acetylene becomes unstable at high pressure. What is the highest working pressure it should be used at?
options: About 5 bar (70 psi)
About 1 bar (15 psi)
About 10 bar (150 psi)
About 3 bar (45 psi)

questions.stem: What is the main job of a brazing flux?
options: To add extra metal so it can fill large gaps
To make the flame burn hotter at the joint
To colour the joint so the inspector can see it
To stop oxides forming so the filler can flow

questions.stem: Silver brazing flux is often a white paste. How can you tell the joint is near the right heat for the filler?
options: The flux turns black and gives off heavy smoke
The flux turns clear and runs like water
The flux dries to a white powder and cracks
The flux bubbles and spits out of the joint

questions.stem: Why must flux left on a brazed joint be washed off after the job?
options: It will melt again in the sun and drip off
It makes the joint look darker than the metal
Most flux left on can corrode the metal
It stops the joint from being painted any colour

questions.stem: A copper-phosphorus brazing rod needs no flux on copper. Which job is it wrong for?
options: Joining mild steel parts
Joining copper water pipe
Joining copper sheet
Joining copper to copper fittings

questions.stem: Brass (bronze) brazing rods are mostly made of which two metals?
options: Tin and lead
Iron and carbon
Aluminium and silicon
Copper and zinc

questions.stem: When choosing a filler metal, how must its melting point compare with the parent metal's?
options: It must be higher than the parent metal's
It must be exactly the same as the parent metal's
It must be lower than the parent metal's
It can be anything if the rod is the same colour

questions.stem: Which joint type gives the strongest brazed joint in thin sheet or tube?
options: A square butt joint with the ends just touching
A lap joint with a good overlap
A tee joint with a wide gap at the root
An open corner joint with no overlap

questions.stem: A common guide for the overlap of a brazed lap joint is about how much?
options: Three times the thickness of the thinner part
Half the thickness of the thinner part
The same as the diameter of the filler rod
One tenth of the whole length of the longer part

questions.stem: What joint gap lets capillary action work in a silver-brazed joint?
options: A wide gap of about 3–5 mm, packed with rod
No gap at all; the parts are pressed in tight
A gap that gets wider from one end to the other
A small, even gap of a fraction of a millimetre

questions.stem: Why must the joint surfaces be cleaned before brazing?
options: So the parts weigh less and are easier to hold
Dirt, grease and oxide stop the filler bonding
So the flux can be left out on clean metal
So the parts will fit together more loosely

questions.stem: Which is a good way to clean copper tube before silver brazing?
options: Rub it bright with emery cloth or fine wire wool
Wipe it with a greasy rag to protect it
Dip it in water and leave it to dry out in the sun
Paint it with primer so it does not tarnish

questions.stem: Why are the parts held with clamps, wire or a jig while they are brazed?
options: So the parts can be heated without any flux
So the parts stay cold while the filler is added
So they keep the right line and gap while heated
So the torch can rest on the clamp while working

questions.stem: Which flame is normally used for silver brazing with oxy-acetylene?
options: A strongly oxidising flame with a short, hissing cone
A flame of acetylene alone, with no oxygen added
A very harsh flame, turned up as high as it will go
A neutral or slightly reducing (soft) flame

questions.stem: When heating a brazed joint, where should most of the heat go?
options: Straight onto the filler rod, to melt it fast
Onto the parent metal, which then melts the rod
Only onto the flux, until it turns black
Onto the clamps holding the parts together

questions.stem: You are brazing a thin copper tube into a heavy brass fitting. Which part should get more of the heat?
options: The thin copper tube
The filler rod
The heavy brass fitting
Both parts exactly the same

questions.stem: Melted filler metal tends to flow in which direction in a joint?
options: Towards the hotter part of the joint
Towards the colder part of the joint
Always straight down, away from the heat
Always back to where the rod first touched

questions.stem: What happens if a silver-brazed joint is badly overheated?
options: The filler flows further and the joint gets stronger
The flux works better and the joint comes out cleaner
The filler sets more quickly and needs no cleaning
The flux burns black and the filler stops flowing

questions.stem: Why should the flame be kept moving while the joint is heated?
options: To stop the flux turning clear too soon
To blow the melted filler right along the joint
To heat the area evenly and avoid hot spots
To keep the gas hose cool behind the torch

questions.stem: When is the filler rod touched onto the joint?
options: Before any heat at all is put on the parts
When the joint is hot enough to melt it
When the flux has burnt black all over
After the parts have cooled down again

questions.stem: Why must a brazed part be left still until the filler has set?
options: Moving it while it sets can crack the joint
Moving it turns the flux into a hard glass
Moving it will make the flame go out at once
Moving it pulls more filler into the gap

questions.stem: After silver brazing a copper part, which is a common way to help remove the flux?
options: Leave it in a dry bin for a week
Paint over the flux with oil paint
Heat it again until the flux burns off
Soak and scrub it in hot water

questions.stem: Which is a sign of a good brazed lap joint?
options: Filler sitting in round lumps on top of the joint
A smooth, even fillet showing all round the joint
Black, burnt flux all over the outside of the joint
Parent metal that has melted and sagged

questions.stem: Filler has balled up on the surface and not run into the joint. What is the most likely cause?
options: The joint had a small, even gap
The flux was the right type for the metal
The parent metal was not hot enough
The parts were cleaned before fitting

questions.stem: In a brazed joint, what are gaps or holes where the filler did not fill the joint called?
options: Undercut
Spatter
Arc strikes
Voids

questions.stem: A brazed copper water pipe must be tested before it goes into use. Which is a simple test?
options: Fill it with water under pressure and check for leaks
Hit it hard with a hammer and listen to see if it rings
Bend it back and forth several times until it breaks
Heat it again and watch how the colour changes

questions.stem: How should a hot brazed part be handled after the job?
options: With bare hands once the colour has gone
With pliers or tongs, and marked as hot
With a damp rag wrapped around it
By picking it up quickly with gloves off

questions.stem: At the end of the day, after the torch valves are closed, what is the next step?
options: Leave the cylinder valves open for the next class
Take the regulators off with the gas still on
Close the cylinder valves, then bleed the hoses
Coil the hoses tightly around the hot torch

questions.stem: What should be done with short rod ends and flux scraps at the end of the job?
options: Put them in the bin the Centre's rules say
Sweep them into the drain outside the workshop
Leave them on the bench for the next group
Burn them on the brazing hearth with the flame

questions.stem: Juliet burns her hand on a hot brazed part. What is the right first aid?
options: Put butter or cooking oil on the burn straight away
Burst any blisters and wrap the hand tightly
Rub ice hard on the burn for half an hour
Hold it under cool running water for 10–20 minutes

questions.stem: You find that a hose on the brazing set is cracked. What should you do?
options: Wrap it with tape and carry on with the job
Tag the set out of use and tell the instructor
Turn the gas pressure down and use it with care
Swap it with the hose from another student's set

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for the metal that is melted into a brazed joint to fill and join it?
Which gas is mixed with acetylene in the torch to make a very hot flame?
Fuel gas fittings have either a left-hand or a right-hand thread. Which one?
Name the white powder, a compound of boron, that is the base of many brass brazing fluxes.
What do the letters PPE stand for?
What is it called when melted filler spreads out evenly and sticks to clean metal?
What device on the cylinder lowers the high cylinder pressure to a low working pressure?
What is the name of the small, bright inner part of an oxy-acetylene flame?
What colour is the fuel gas (acetylene) hose?
Name the bottled gas, also used for cooking in Jamaica, that is often burned in air-fuel brazing torches.
What name is given to the metal of the parts being joined, as opposed to the filler?
What tool should be used to light a gas torch, instead of matches or a cigarette lighter?
What is the name of the process where a brass rod builds up a fillet like a weld, without relying on capillary flow?
Bronze is mainly copper mixed with which other metal?
What document from the supplier gives the hazards of a flux and how to handle it safely?

essays.stem: Describe the personal protective equipment and the workshop precautions needed for oxy-fuel brazing and silver soldering. Say why each one is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: Wear tinted goggles or a visor of about shade 3 to 5 to cut the glare from the flame and the hot flux and to stop sparks reaching the eyes. Wear leather gloves and a long-sleeved cotton or leather jacket, buttoned up, because hot metal, flux and sparks burn the skin, and nylon melts onto it. Wear safety boots with the trousers over them. Work with good ventilation or fume extraction, because flux fumes and zinc or cadmium fumes harm the lungs; use cadmium-free filler. Clear away anything that can burn, work on firebricks or a fire-resistant bench, and keep an extinguisher close. Keep the cylinders upright and chained, with flashback arrestors fitted. Handle hot parts with tongs and mark them hot. Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Tinted goggles or visor (about shade 3 to 5) against glare, heat and sparks
Leather gloves, flame-resistant long-sleeved clothing and boots, against burns
Ventilation or extraction for flux and metal fumes; cadmium-free filler
Fire precautions: burnables cleared, fire-resistant surface, extinguisher at hand
Cylinders secured with arrestors fitted; hot parts handled with tongs and marked

essays.stem: Describe how to set up an oxy-acetylene set for brazing, from the cylinders to lighting the torch.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that both cylinders are upright and chained to the trolley or wall. Check that the valve outlets are clean and free of oil, and stand to one side when a valve is opened. Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the acetylene regulator (left-hand thread), then fit flashback arrestors on the regulator outlets. Check the hoses for cracks, cuts or burns, and connect them the right way: oxygen hose to oxygen, red hose to fuel gas, with non-return valves at the torch. Fit the right nozzle for the job. Open the cylinder valves slowly and set the working pressures from the maker's chart. Test every joint with soapy water. Purge each hose for a few seconds. Open the fuel valve a little, light it with a spark lighter, then add oxygen to get the flame needed.
markingPoints: Cylinders upright and secured; outlets clean and oil-free; stands aside and opens valves slowly
Regulators fitted to the right gas (fuel left-hand, oxygen right-hand) with flashback arrestors
Hoses checked and connected the right way; suitable nozzle fitted
Pressures set from the maker's chart; leak test with soapy water; hoses purged
Lights the fuel gas first with a spark lighter, then adds oxygen to set the flame

essays.stem: Explain how to prepare a copper tube and a copper fitting (a socket joint) for silver brazing.
essays.modelAnswer: First cut the tube square with a tube cutter, and remove the burr inside and out so that the tube goes fully into the socket and the flow inside the pipe is not blocked. Check the fit: there should be a small, even gap all round, a fraction of a millimetre, so that capillary action can draw the filler in. Clean the outside of the tube end and the inside of the socket to bright metal with emery cloth or a fitting brush. Do not touch the cleaned surfaces with greasy fingers. Brush a thin coat of the right flux onto the cleaned tube end, push it fully into the socket and turn it to spread the flux. Support the parts so that they stay in line and do not move while they are heated. Have the filler ready and the area clear.
markingPoints: Cuts the tube square and removes the burr
Checks for a small, even gap for capillary flow
Cleans both surfaces to bright metal and keeps grease off
Applies a thin coat of the correct flux and assembles the joint fully
Supports or clamps the parts so they stay in line while heated

essays.stem: Compare brazing with brass rod, silver soldering and soft soldering. Say how they differ in temperature, filler metal, strength and typical jobs.
essays.modelAnswer: In all three the parent metal does not melt: a filler metal flows into the joint and bonds to the surfaces. Soft soldering uses a tin-based solder that melts below 450 °C. It is quick and needs little heat, but the joint is weak, so it is used for electrical work and light sealing jobs. Silver soldering (silver brazing) uses a silver-bearing alloy that melts above 450 °C, often at about 600–800 °C. It flows well into close-fitting joints and gives a strong, neat joint, so it is used for copper pipe, refrigeration lines and small steel or brass parts. Brass (bronze) brazing uses a copper-zinc rod at a higher heat, about 900 °C, with a borax-type flux. It gives a strong joint, can fill wider gaps, and is used on steel frames and on some repairs.
markingPoints: In all three the filler melts and the parent metal does not
Soft solder melts below 450 °C, gives a weak joint, used for light or electrical work
Silver solder melts above 450 °C (about 600–800 °C), strong, close gaps, copper pipe and fine work
Brass brazing at about 900 °C with borax-type flux, strong, used on steel
Gives a correct typical job for each process

essays.stem: Describe step by step how to silver braze a copper tube into a copper fitting, from lighting the torch to cleaning the finished joint.
essays.modelAnswer: Light the torch and set a neutral or slightly soft flame of a size that suits the fitting. Heat the tube first, then move the flame onto the fitting, keeping it moving so that the whole joint heats evenly. Watch the flux: it bubbles, then turns clear and runs like water, which shows that the joint is near the right heat. Touch the filler rod to the joint at the edge of the socket, on the side away from the flame, and let the hot metal melt it. The filler is drawn into the gap and shows as a thin, bright ring all round. Take the flame away and keep the joint still until the filler has set. Let it cool, then wash and brush off the flux with hot water. Check that there is a full ring of filler.
markingPoints: Neutral or soft flame; heats the whole joint evenly with the flame moving
Uses the flux turning clear as the sign of the right heat
Feeds the rod at the joint edge so the hot work melts it and the filler runs all round
Keeps the joint still until the filler sets
Washes off the flux residue and checks for a full ring of filler

essays.stem: Explain why flux is needed for brazing, how the right flux is chosen and put on, and how flux residue and fumes are dealt with.
essays.modelAnswer: When metal is heated in air, a thin oxide layer forms on it, and the filler will not wet or bond to oxide. Flux dissolves the oxide, stops new oxide forming and helps the filler to flow. The flux must suit the filler and the parent metal and must work at the brazing heat: for example, a borax-type flux for brass brazing and a silver brazing flux, usually a white paste, for silver solder. Some copper-phosphorus rods need no flux on copper. Read the label and the safety data sheet. Clean the joint first, then brush a thin, even coat of flux just where the filler must go. Many fluxes give off harmful fumes when hot, so work with good ventilation or extraction and keep your face out of the fumes. After brazing, wash off the residue with hot water and a brush, because it is corrosive.
markingPoints: Oxide stops wetting; flux removes and prevents oxide and helps the filler flow
Flux chosen to match the filler, the metal and the temperature, with an example
Thin coat put on the clean joint where the filler must flow
Ventilation or extraction for flux fumes; reads the label or safety data sheet
Corrosive residue washed off after brazing

essays.stem: Explain how you control the heat when brazing two parts of different thickness, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Filler only flows into a joint where both parts are at brazing heat, and it runs towards the hotter part. A thick part takes longer to heat and draws heat away, while a thin part heats quickly and can overheat. So point most of the flame at the thicker part and only play it briefly over the thin part. Keep the flame moving so that there are no hot spots, and use a flame size that suits the thicker part. Watch the flux on both parts: when it has turned clear on both, the joint is ready. Then feed the filler where the parts meet and let the heat draw it in. If the thin part is overheated, the flux burns black, oxide forms and the filler will not flow, and thin metal may even melt.
markingPoints: Both parts must reach brazing heat; the filler flows towards the heat
Most heat on the thicker part, brief heat on the thin part
Flame kept moving, with a size that suits the job
Flux on both parts watched as the sign that the joint is ready
Explains what overheating the thin part does

essays.stem: Name four faults that can be found in brazed or silver-soldered joints. For each, give one cause and one way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Voids or lack of fill: the filler has not run right through the joint. It is caused by a dirty joint, a gap that is too wide or too tight, or uneven heat. Prevent it by cleaning well, setting a small, even gap and heating the whole joint. Filler balling on the surface: the parent metal was too cold, so the rod melted in the flame instead. Heat the parent metal until the flux runs clear and let it melt the rod. Burnt, black flux and a rough joint: the joint was overheated or heated for too long. Use the right flame size and keep it moving. Cracks or a weak joint: the parts moved while the filler was setting. Clamp or support the parts and keep them still until the filler has set.
markingPoints: Voids or lack of fill, with a correct cause and prevention
Filler balling or poor flow from cold parent metal, with prevention
Overheating and burnt flux, with prevention
Cracks or weak joint from movement, with prevention
Uses correct trade terms and links causes to cleaning, fit-up, heat or support

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan a brazing job before you start: what you check on the drawing, how you choose the process, filler and flux, and how you prepare the work area.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the drawing and the job sheet to find the parent metals, the sizes, the joint type and how strong or leak-tight the joint must be. Ask the instructor about anything that is not clear. Then choose the process: silver soldering for copper pipe and small close-fitting parts, or brass brazing for steel parts. Choose a filler that melts well below the parent metal and a flux that suits both the filler and the metal, and read their labels and safety data sheets. Choose a torch or nozzle size to suit the thickness. Collect the tools: cleaning cloth, flux brush, clamps and tongs. Prepare the area: firebricks or a fire-resistant bench, good ventilation, burnables removed and an extinguisher at hand. Check the gas equipment before lighting up.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and job sheet for metals, sizes, joint type and what the joint must do
Chooses a suitable process, filler and flux, and reads the labels or data sheets
Chooses the torch or nozzle size and collects the tools
Prepares a safe area: fire-resistant surface, ventilation, burnables cleared, extinguisher
Checks the gas equipment before starting

essays.stem: Describe how you shut down the gas equipment and leave the work area safe at the end of a brazing job, and say what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: Close the torch valves in the order the maker gives and hang the torch up away from the cylinders. Close both cylinder valves. Open the torch valves one at a time to bleed the gas out of the hoses until both gauges read zero, then close them, and wind out the regulator adjusting screws. Coil the hoses loosely, with no kinks, away from hot metal. Leave brazed parts to cool, or handle them with tongs and mark them hot. Wash off any flux residue. Put rod ends and flux waste in the right bin, put the lids back on flux pots and return filler and tools to the store. Check the area for smouldering fires before leaving. Report any damaged hose, leaking fitting, faulty regulator or near miss to the instructor, and tag faulty equipment out of use.
markingPoints: Torch valves closed in the maker's order, then the cylinder valves
Hoses bled to zero, regulator screws released and hoses coiled
Hot parts handled with tongs and marked; flux residue washed off
Waste in the right bin, consumables stored, area checked for fire
Faults and near misses reported, and faulty equipment tagged out of use

practical1.title: Silver brazing a small copper pipe assembly
practical1.brief: As a group, silver braze a small pipe assembly in 15 mm copper tube: a short run with one tee and two elbows, with end caps on two outlets and one end left open for filling. Plan the joints together, then share them out so that every member cuts, cleans, fluxes and brazes at least two joints while the assessor watches. One member sets up the gas equipment while the others check each step, and every member helps with the water test. When the assembly is cool, wash off the flux, fill it with water through the open end, leave it for 10 minutes and check every joint for drips. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 15 mm copper fittings: 1 tee, 2 elbows, 2 end caps
Cadmium-free silver brazing alloy and the matching flux
Tube cutter, deburring tool, emery cloth or fitting brushes
Oxy-acetylene or air-propane torch set with flashback arrestors, and a spark lighter
Firebricks, tongs, a bucket of hot water and a scrubbing brush
photos: The work area set up: firebricks, extinguisher and ventilation, with every member in PPE
Tube ends cut, deburred and cleaned, laid out with the fittings
Flux applied and the parts assembled before heating
A joint being brazed, with the ring of filler showing
The finished assembly after the flux has been washed off
The water test, showing every joint dry
The work area cleaned and the gas equipment shut down
checklist: Wore tinted goggles or a visor, leather gloves and cotton or leather clothing throughout
Checked the gas equipment (cylinders secured, arrestors fitted, leak test) before lighting
Cut the tube square, removed the burr and cleaned both surfaces to bright metal
Put on a thin, even coat of the right flux and pushed the joint fully home
Heated the joint evenly and fed the filler only when the flux ran clear
Own joints show a full, even ring of filler with no gaps or burnt flux
Washed off the flux, and own joints passed the water test with no drips
Shut down the gas safely and left the area clean, with waste in the right bin
safety: Use cadmium-free filler; braze only with good ventilation or extraction, and keep your face out of the fumes
Keep cylinders upright and chained; check for leaks with soapy water, never with a flame
Clear away anything that can burn; work on firebricks and keep an extinguisher at hand
Treat all brazed parts as hot: use tongs and mark them hot
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for the torch, filler and flux

practical2.title: Brass brazing lap joints in mild steel sheet, with a peel test
practical2.brief: As a group, set up and leak test an oxy-acetylene set, then braze lap joints in 1.5 mm mild steel sheet with brass (bronze) brazing rod and a borax-type flux. Each member cleans and brazes one lap joint (two pieces about 100 mm × 50 mm with an overlap of about 10 mm) on firebricks, using the flame setting the instructor gives for brass rod. Then the group cuts a strip across one extra joint and peels it apart in the vice to see how far the filler ran into the overlap. Each member tells the assessor what the peel test shows. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 1.5 mm mild steel sheet cut to about 100 mm × 50 mm (2 pieces per member, plus 2 for the peel test)
Borax-type brazing flux, or flux-coated rods
Oxy-acetylene set with flashback arrestors, a nozzle chart and a spark lighter
Emery cloth or wire brush, firebricks, tongs and small clamps
Bench vice, pliers and a hacksaw for the peel test
photos: The gas set up and leak tested, with every member in PPE
The sheets cleaned and set up as a lap joint on firebricks
Flux on and the joint being heated
A finished lap joint, top view
The peel-test strip pulled apart, showing how far the filler spread
The work area cleaned and the gas equipment shut down
checklist: Wore suitable PPE throughout, including tinted goggles and leather gloves
Helped to set up and leak test the gas set, and lit and adjusted the flame safely
Cleaned the sheet to bright metal and set the lap joint with the right overlap
Heated the steel to a dull red and let the hot work melt the rod
Made an even, continuous braze along the joint with no burnt flux or melted sheet
Took part in the peel test and explained what it shows about filler flow
Shut down the gas safely and left the area tidy
safety: Brass rod gives off zinc fumes: work with ventilation or extraction and keep your head out of the fumes
Keep cylinders upright and chained; check for leaks with soapy water
Work on firebricks, with burnables cleared and an extinguisher at hand
Wear gloves for the peel test: the torn edges are sharp
Use tongs for hot parts and mark them hot; follow the Centre's rules for hot work
